column4: Trumpet blowing pressure and radiated level for three players: threshold p0 = K f with K = 7, 8 and 4 Pa/Hz (Eq. 1, Fig 4), loud playing at 3.3 to 3.9 times threshold (Fig 6: C4 2.0 / 3.9 / 6.6, C5 3.3 / 6.3 / 13.0, C6 6.7 / 11.0 / 24.0 kPa), A-weighted SPL at 1 m against blowing pressure per note (Figs 1 and 2), and the frequency above which the radiated envelope is 20 dB under its peak (Fig 9)
column14: N. H. Fletcher and A. Tarnopolsky, Blowing pressure, power, and spectrum in trumpet playing, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 105(2) 874-881 (1999); the DOI was not verified by this lane. Used as a PLAYER INPUT of the trumpet render recipe (descriptions/trumpet/render.sh): threshold p0 = K f with K = 7 Pa/Hz for the professional player GC (8 for NH, 4 for KB; Eq. 1 and Fig 4, p.877) and loud playing at 3.3 to 3.9 times threshold (Fig 6), so the held notes use 3.5 x 7 Pa/Hz x f: 5.71, 8.56, 11.42 and 14.39 kPa for Bb3, F4, Bb4 and D5. The A-weighted SPL at 1 m against pressure per note (Fig 1 GC anechoic, Fig 2 NH living room; players differ by about 3 dB) and the 20 dB cutoff frequency (Fig 9) were READ BY EYE from the figures on a 300 dpi raster with their gridlines (about 1 dB) and are used only as diagnostic comparators on the status card, never as targets or inputs. Different trumpets and players from the Iowa recordings.

column4: Mechanical response of in vivo trombonists' lips formed into embouchures (frontal high-speed video under a calibrated acoustic sweep): outward-striking resonance 32 to 60 Hz with Q 1.5 to 2.4 over the target notes Bb1 to F3 and a second resonance with Q 1.2 to 5, printed per player and target note in Sec. 4.4 and summarised in Table 4.2
column14: M. J. Newton, PhD thesis, University of Edinburgh 2009, Sec. 4.4.1 to 4.4.3 and Table 4.2 (the thesis' own sentences and table; no figure was read). Two experienced trombonists, AJ and TJ. A SYSTEM response of the whole embouchure (lips, mouthpiece, acoustic drive), stored under apparatus-effective names and usable only through a forward model of that apparatus, never as a tissue modulus. Stated uncertainty: peak-frequency repeatability about 10 percent (about 5 percent for TJ at Bb2); Q by a damped-oscillator fit that the thesis says is less accurate than on artificial lips. The printed Table 4.2 second-resonance range (70 to 100 Hz) does not match the second resonances printed in the text (140 to 200 Hz); both are kept. The published form is Newton, Campbell and Gilbert, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 123(1) 2008, whose abstract (a search result only; the full text was not opened) says four semi-professional players, where the thesis text used here says two. For scale: Cullen's artificial lips (ledger row cullen-2000-artificial-lip-parameters) have an outward resonance 204.5 to 237.0 Hz with Q 7 to 12, which is about 3 to 7 times higher in frequency and about 3 to 8 times higher in Q than these human embouchure values.

column4: Initial Young's modulus from an in vivo aspiration device with Neo-Hookean inverse analysis on 16 young subjects: lower lip 33.7 +- 7.3 kPa, cheek 31.0 +- 4.6, cheekbone 34.9 +- 6.6, forehead 17.3 +- 4.1
column14: V. Luboz, E. Promayon and Y. Payan, Annals of Biomedical Engineering 42(11) 2369-2378 (2014), the abstract read verbatim through the Europe PMC REST API (PMID 25186433); the publisher copy was not opened. An effective value of an aspiration apparatus acting on a layered face (skin, fat, muscle, and at the lip mucosa and orbicularis oris), not an intrinsic modulus of any layer: stored under apparatus-effective names. The abstract does not say whether the +- is a standard deviation or a standard error. Strauss (arXiv 2404.05056) quotes the lower-lip value as an ultrasonic measurement; the abstract says aspiration.

column4: Perioral (mouth-corner interangle) stiffness of relaxed lips of 20 healthy young males over a 24 mm stretch: quadratic regression of the stiffness coefficient on interangle span, 0.0767 - 0.0030 S + 0.0005 S^2 N/mm (R-squared 58 percent), and the female equation 0.0945 - 0.0055 S + 0.0005 S^2 (R-squared 77 percent) quoted from Seibel and Barlow 2007
column14: S.-Y. Chu, S. M. Barlow and J. Lee, J. Speech Lang. Hear. Res. 2009, Eqs. 2 and 3, Fig 4 and Tables 1 and 2, read from the PMC author manuscript through NCBI efetch. A lateral stiffness of the perioral system at the mouth corners, not the transverse stiffness of the vibrating lip: apparatus-effective. The unit of the regression variable Interangle_Span is not stated where it is defined; this lane reads it as mm of stretch from rest because the printed step variances imply scores of 0.03 to 0.3 N/mm (an inference, recorded in the pack). Stated uncertainty: R-squared and the within-step variances of Table 1.

column4: OroSTIFF, a face-referenced device: estimated mean perioral stiffness over all trials and participants 0.073 N/mm (SE 0.002), 10 male and 10 female healthy adults, relaxed lips, stiffness from the force change over a 1 mm change during elastic recoil
column14: S.-Y. Chu, S. M. Barlow, D. Kieweg and J. Lee, J. Biomech. 2010, Results, read from the PMC author manuscript through NCBI efetch. Perioral lateral stiffness of the mouth corners, apparatus-effective. Stated uncertainty: SE 0.002 N/mm on the mean, and a variance split that puts almost all variability within participants.

column4: An estimate of lip-tissue elasticity from the lip waves of horn players (Acta Acustica united with Acustica 89:145-162, 2003)
column14: Known only from the reference list of Newton's thesis and a search result; the paper sits behind the publisher's paywall and was not opened, so no number from it is used. The title says it estimates lip-tissue elasticity from horn players' lip-wave measurements, which makes it the only lip-specific constitutive estimate this lane has a pointer to besides the apparatus responses above. Request through the publisher or the authors.

column4: Ogden (1972) three-term decoupled strain-energy coefficients fitted to Treloar's 1944 rubber data: exponents 1.3, 5.0 and -2.0 with coefficients 0.63, 0.0012 and -0.01 MPa; Table I of Twizell and Ogden 1981 prints 6.3, 0.012 and -0.1 for the same exponents, with no unit
column14: R. W. Ogden, Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A 326 (1972) 565-584, doi:10.1098/rspa.1972.0026: the original was not opened by this lane, and the code's author recorded that access to it was blocked (commit cb9fc0a73). Read this session instead: E. H. Twizell and R. W. Ogden, Non-linear optimization of the material constants in Ogden's strain-energy function (Brunel University report TR/05/81, 1981, open access), Table I row Ogden (1972): coefficients 6.3, -0.1 and 0.012 for exponents 1.3, -2.0 and 5.0 (the code orders its terms by 1.3, 5.0, -2.0). The report prints no unit. The code's 0.63, 0.0012 and -0.01 MPa (Holzapfel 2000 Sec. 6.5 per the code comment) are 0.1 MPa per printed unit; if the printed unit is kgf/cm2, Treloar's unit (an inference), the exact factor is 0.0980665, a 2 percent difference in absolute scale that cannot affect the gates, because the law and the analytic oracle use the same coefficients. Table II of the same report gives a sum of squares of 302.9 for this set against simple-tension data, so it is a coarse fit there. Used as a reference curve without refit; stated uncertainty: none.

column4: Treloar (1944) stress-strain observations of vulcanised natural rubber as printed in Table A1 of Appendix A of Bucchi and Hearn (2013): 22 uniaxial, 16 equibiaxial and 13 pure-shear points (engineering strain and stress in Pa)
column14: A. Bucchi and G. W. Hearn, Predictions of aneurysm formation in distensible tubes, Part A, Appendix A, Table A1 (author manuscript on the University of Portsmouth research portal). Typed by the code's author (commit cb9fc0a73). This lane could not re-open the manuscript (the portal answers non-browser requests with HTTP 403; not bypassed) and screened the typed values against the Ogden-1972 analytic curve instead: the deviations are smooth (uniaxial at most 13.7 percent, pure shear 15.8, equibiaxial 47 percent only at lambda 1.02 where the stress is tiny), with no outlier that points at a typing error. How Bucchi and Hearn obtained the values from Treloar (1944) (retrieval from his tables or digitization of his figures) is not stated in what this lane saw, and neither is any uncertainty or fit band, so the row is a fixture: the points are logged against the law by the test and gated by nothing. Treloar's own paper (Trans. Faraday Soc. 40:59) was not opened.

column4: Holzapfel, Gasser and Ogden (2000) fibre-reinforced model parameters for the media of their Fig. 14: c = 3 kPa, k1 = 2.3632 kPa, k2 = 0.8393 (the code's c10 is c/2)
column14: G. A. Holzapfel, T. C. Gasser and R. W. Ogden, J. Elasticity 61 (2000) 1-48. The numbers were verified against the primary PDF by the code's author (commit cb9fc0a73: HGO Fig14 primary PDF verified); this lane did not re-open the paper (publisher paywall), so the tissue and the test data behind the figure are not restated here. Used as a reference parameter set without refit by the HGO uniaxial analytic gates; stated uncertainty: none.

column4: Force on the perioral structures of 28 wind music students measured with piezoresistive (FlexiForce) sensors on the mouthpiece, per instrument and sensor (upper or lower lip, incisors for single reed), mean medium and maximum over nine trials: trumpet (6 players) upper sensor medium 62.7 g (SD 10.9), maximum 130.3 g (SD 54.2), lower sensor medium 89.2 g (SD 97.3), maximum 172.3 g (SD 141.0); trombone and French horn one player each; clarinet, saxophone, bassoon, oboe and flutes
column14: M. P. Clemente, A. Moreira, J. Mendes, A. P. Ferreira and J. M. Amarante, Wind Instrumentalist Embouchure and the Applied Forces on the Perioral Structures, The Open Dentistry Journal 13 (2019), e-location TODENTJ-13-107, CC BY 4.0; Tables 1 to 7 typed from the open-access HTML text, with the abstract and the methods read. Players were master's students in music performance (not professionals as a group); the sensors were on the mouthpiece against the external zone of the lips for brass, so the values are mouthpiece-lip contact forces as seen by a thin sensor, a boundary condition for a lip model and not a tissue property. Force is printed in g with no newton or kPa value; the calibration used weights, so this lane reads g as gram-force (an inference). Stated uncertainty: the standard deviation across the players of the group for the group tables; the trombone and the horn are one player each (Table 5 single values). Printed inconsistencies kept: Table 2 saxophone upper sensor maximum has a minimum 43 above its maximum 16; the Discussion says the trombone reached up to 330 g where Table 5 gives 325 g; the abstract gives the bisel flute maximum as 245 g where Table 7 gives 249 g. The sensor placement for brass is described only in words and Fig. 3, not as a position on the lip; the individual note pitches are not stated.

column14: Derived output of bowed_card_sweep (landed 601e374fc, built at 6f2e42ec7 on trj, one host, nice-d): each card's string, damping and friction records (checked identical to the committed cards) at relative bow position 1/11 and bow speed 0.15 m/s, rigid bridge, 1 s runs from rest at constant force on a geometric force grid; a second 'ext' grid extends the cello and bass cards upward. Classes are the gate detector's declared rig tolerances, not literature constants; the sweep starts from rest at constant speed, so it maps the steady regime reached from a step onset and measures neither the onset transient nor hysteresis. The cards' bow forces are derived from these receipts (descriptions sources.tsv). Not instrument-fidelity data; no measured-limit comparison is claimed.

column4: Monochord D and E strings of the 2008 bowing-machine study as sweep cards, their measured Helmholtz force limits (Table VII), and the model's own limits on the same strings
column14: E. Schoonderwaldt, K. Guettler, A. Askenfelt, Acta Acustica united with Acustica 94 (2008) 604-622, sec. 2.1 (string length, string data), Table VI (Q1) and Table VII (c_upper, c_lower with standard errors at 10 cm/s) transcribed by hand from the PDF text. Sweeps by bowed_card_sweep at 6f2e42ec7 (rigid bridge, step onset, one host). The limits table compares the model's lowest and highest Helmholtz forces with the measured F_min and F_max under the detector's declared rig tolerances, which are not the paper's classification. Torsion, which the paper says lowers F_max, and per-mode damping are absent. No figure data digitised.

column4: Clare D tin whistle measured by ISVR: bore 12.2 mm and wall 0.3 mm, brass tube 259 mm in a 59 mm plastic mouthpiece, six hole diameters and centre spacings, resonator length 267.3 mm from the window centre, flue channel 8 mm wide tapering from 2 to 1.48 mm over 24.55 mm, window 5.3 by 8 mm with 2.4 mm wall, 8 mm wedge about 25 degrees, 8 mm closed pocket behind the flue; staging of the tone with flow rate
column14: P. O. A. L. Davies, J. Pinho and E. J. English, Some acoustic characteristics of the tin whistle, Proceedings of the Institute of Acoustics 28(1), 2006, pp. 597-606 (ISVR repository copy, personal use, not retained). Sec. 3 geometry text (values are averages, the tube and the holes were not quite round), Eq. 5 open-end correction, Eq. 10 hole model; Fig. 1 and 2 flow rates of the overblown series, Table 1 flow rate and frequency per note. Measured in an anechoic room at 20 C; humidity unstated.

column4: Air flow rates at which the Clare D whistle sounds each note of the D major scale at its tempered frequency (l/min: D5 6.2, E5 6.9, F#5 9.0, G5 8.2, A5 10.0, B5 9.55, C#6 11.3, D6 with hole 6 open 11.9, D6 closed 12) and the overblown series with all holes closed (D5 6.1, D6 12.0, A6 17.9, D7 23.8; the flows are near exact multiples of the harmonic order)
column14: Same paper as isvr-davies-2006-tin-whistle: Table 1 (columns frequency, holes open, flow rate) and Figure 2 captions. A regulated metered air supply and a player routinely adjusting flow; the 6.1 and 6.2 l/min of D5 differ between the figure and the table. The recipe converts flow to mouth pressure with the island's viscous windway law.

column4: Fingering chart of the D major scale on the six-hole tin whistle: which holes are closed or open for each note from D5 to the upper D (the upper D has only the hole nearest the mouth open)
column14: J. Timoney, T. Lysaght, L. Mac Manus and A. Schwarzbacher, Timbral attributes for objective quality assessment of the Irish tin whistle, Proc. 7th Int. Conference on Digital Audio Effects (DAFx'04), Naples, 2004, Fig. 2 (open and filled dots read by eye, categorical, no numerical error). The paper of the whistle measurements (Sec. 3.2) states the same cleaner D6 fingering with holes 1 to 5 covered and hole 6 open. Reading error (OD17): the quantity is categorical (open or filled dot per hole and note), so there is no numerical error; the bound is a misread dot. The cleaner D6 fingering (holes 1 to 5 covered, hole 6 open) is cross-checked against the text of the ISVR paper Sec. 3.2; the other notes are not independently cross-checked. The source states no error.

column4: Authored flue performance inputs of the tin whistle built from the published geometry and the published flow rates: mouth pressure of each note from its flow through Shah's laminar developing-flow law of the measured flue (windway slit-developing), the network, the render recipe and the status card
column14: A fixture for listening, not graded: no licensed reference recording exists (bead pexfp.219). Authored items: onset ramp 50 ms, jet displacement gain 90, the repository interim slot-jet card, labium offset and jet angle zero (UNKNOWN), dry air. The overblown-series files d6c, a6c, d7c are the paper's measured operating points. Pressures (pexfp.135.4 W1, ruling 8741): derived from the ISVR measured flows through Shah's developing-flow law (e2414832f), each held note inside the law's cited validity (render.sh lists the measures). The law's cross-code check against Segoufin's laminar RNS-p straight channel (thesis Fig. 5.14) is laminar vs laminar: it verifies the law in x+ only, and laminarity is bounded separately by the cited criteria. The thesis states two Reynolds length scales, so its status is split: MET under Re_Dh = 2 Re (2/2), MISSED under Re_Dh = 4 Re (1/3; 7 to 9 % low at a6c's x+, with d7c below the graded range). Chen's K(inf) = 0.64 + 38/Re and Shah and London's agreement statement behind the x+ floor are secondary, search snippet only; primary not read.

column4: Panpipe acoustics: pipe diameter against length d = 1.32 L^0.43 (mm) of Eastern European panpipes, jet speed 20 to 40 m/s, initial jet half-width 0.5 to 1 mm, jet length 5 to 10 mm shorter for high notes, jet spreading half-angle about 6 degrees, and the stopped-pipe jet offset of about 0.5 jet half-widths (Eq. 6, alpha 2, gamma 0.4)
column14: N. H. Fletcher, Stopped-pipe wind instruments: Acoustics of the panpipes, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 117(1), 2005, pp. 370-374 (UNSW web copy, personal use, not retained). Sec. II (scaling, Fig. 2), Sec. IV (aerodynamics, Eq. 5 to 9), Sec. VI (higher notes use a shorter jet, a higher pressure and a lower lip opening). One Peruvian panpipe showed a similar but much less regular scaling. No table of tube lengths.

Ghezzi, Diseno de una zampona con tubos de vidrio, Revista Boliviana de Fisica 17, 47-52 (2010), Sec. 2 and Table 1 (theoretical frequencies, A at 440 Hz; their octave labels are shifted by one from scientific pitch). column4: Authored flue performance inputs of the pan pipes built from published rules: tube lengths computed from the note set, bore from the published regression, blowing pressure and jet length from Fletcher 1975's measured flute-player relations at each tube's pitch (fletcher-1975-flute-blowing-pressure-and-jet-length), lip height from the published range ends paired linearly in log2 f, the cited stopped-pipe offset, the network, the render recipe and the status card

column4: Blowing pressure and jet length of four experienced flute players against the frequency of the note: the median blowing pressure in excess of atmospheric p [mbar] = 0.008 nu [Hz], the maximum observed deviation mostly +-50 %, the same relation for one player on the alto (G) flute (Eq. 1, p. 233); the median jet length l [mm] = 1.8 + 100 nu^(-1/2), all measurements within about +-20 %, the players making little or no adjustment with dynamic level (Eq. 2, p. 234); and, from the same data with a dead interval of 1.8 mm shielded from the acoustic field, (l - 1.8 mm) p^(-1/2) = 1100 / nu in mbar, mm and Hz (Eq. 5, p. 235, not used). The pan-pipe cards take Eq. 1 for the blowing pressure and Eq. 2 for the cut-up (jet length) at each tube's equal-tempered pitch
column14: N. H. Fletcher, Acoustical correlates of flute performance technique, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 57(1) 1975 pp. 233-237 (ANU open repository copy), read in full, Figs. 1 and 2 viewed for this row. Pressure was measured with a 1 mm catheter in one corner of the lip opening connected to an aneroid gauge calibrated against a water column; jet length from profile photographs, from the apparent point of emergence of the jet at the lips to the target edge. The plotted measurements span C4 (262 Hz) to about C7; the alto-flute statement has no plotted data. The source says its jet-length data cannot distinguish Eq. 2 from a simple linear relation between l and nu: the form is assumed from a derivation given later in the paper. These are FLUTE players. Fletcher 2005 (fletcher-2005-panpipes-jasa) cites this paper as its ref 12 for a jet speed of 'typically about 20-40 m/s depending upon the note' and says the jet is made shorter and the pressure higher for high notes; neither paper measures a pan-pipe or siku player, so using the relations for a stopped pipe is an analogy (unknowns u-player-controls). The pan-pipe cards evaluate the relations at the tempered pitches D3 146.832, G3 195.998, D4 293.665, G4 391.995 and B4 493.883 Hz (A4 = 440 Hz): D3 lies below every pitch reported and G3 is the alto flute's lowest note. 1 mbar = 100 Pa; the card pressure is printed to five significant figures. Companion rows from the same paper: fletcher-1975-coltman-flute-lip-coverage and fletcher-1975-flute-lip-emergence-setback.

column4: Measured input impedance (magnitude, phase, real and imaginary parts) of a Yamaha Custom CX Bb clarinet for 74 fingerings including alternates and multiphonics, 118.4 to 4002.5 Hz at 2.69 Hz, reed compliance excluded; used only as scalar facts: sounding and 0.8 to 2.6 kHz maximum heights for the seven open-hole fingerings of the Buffet comparison

Wolfe, Clarinet acoustics: introducing a compendium of impedance and sound spectra, https://www.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/reprints/AAclarinet.pdf; data page https://www.phys.unsw.edu.au/music/clarinet/ (footer: (c) 1997-2006 Music Acoustics UNSW, no licence or reuse statement). Workbook sheets magnitude, angle, real, imaginary; first row fingering names in WRITTEN pitch (all-holes-closed E3 has its first maximum at 150.7 Hz, concert D3); first column Freq_Hz; no temperature or humidity stated on the page; instrument is a Yamaha Custom CX, neither the Buffet Prestige nor the Yamaha Y250 of the specimens. No curve bytes retained: the file was read once for scalar band-maximum ratios computed by script, and the scalars are quoted in the clarinet status card and bead comments.

column4: Bressan alto recorder 'd' (Frans Brueggen collection, Fred Morgan drawing X): head, middle joint and foot lengths, bore at stations along the three joints, thumb hole and six finger hole positions, sizes and outer diameters, hole 7 diameter, window 12.0 x 4.6 mm, labium lengths and widths, step 0.8 mm, edge thickness, block chamfer, windway length 61.5 mm; window opening height of the Berlin alto e and the opening to exit area ratio; pitch of the alto about a1 = 409 Hz
column14: J. Bouterse, FoMRHI Quarterly Comm. 1929 (Q 118, 2010, Alto recorders by Bressan: bore profiles; Tables 1 to 5), Comm. 1898 (Q 115, 2010, Five alto recorders by Bressan: windways and blocks; window, labium and step tables, the alto e opening and the 1.7 area ratio) and Comm. 1910 (Q 116, 2010, pitch and sound; pitch deviations at a = 415 Hz), reprinted with Comm. 1880 on the author's site (mcjbouterse.nl, Bressan-windways-English-Dutch-Bouterse-combined.pdf); Comm. 2115 (Q 146, 2015) gives the Wijne soprano windway width 10.8 to 8.6 mm for an 8.9 mm window. Terms stated by the author: reprinting, duplication and translation, including excerpts, only with prior written approval and with the source cited, so only the numerical facts are retained and the tables are not reproduced. The data are Bouterse's tabulation of Morgan's drawing of the present, shrunken and slightly oval wood (maxima; Table 5 extrapolated and rounded, +-0.1 mm); the windway height of alto d is NOT given. Hole 7 position not given.

column4: Pressure of the first to second register jump of an alto Bressan Zen-On recorder blown by a pressure-controlled artificial mouth on an increasing ramp, F4, G4, A4, Bb4 and B4 fingerings, and the hysteresis between the increasing and decreasing jumps: increasing thresholds about 230, 255, 305, 505, 490 Pa and hysteresis about 95, 90, 95, 90, 60 Pa (artificial mouth); first-register oscillation near 350 Hz and second near 740 Hz for F4
column14: S. Terrien, R. Blandin, C. Vergez and B. Fabre, Regime change thresholds in recorder-like instruments: influence of the mouth pressure dynamics, Acta Acustica united with Acustica 101 (2015) 300-316 (arXiv non-exclusive licence), Fig. 1 to Fig. 3. Values read by eye from plotted points, error about 20 Pa. The recorder's geometry is described in their reference [16] (Lyons 1981) and is not retained. Used only to set the pressure of four held first-register notes (the decreasing threshold: increasing threshold minus hysteresis); the crescendos choose no pressure. Reading error (OD17): each threshold and hysteresis value read by eye from the plotted points of Fig. 1 to Fig. 3 of the arXiv copy, no pixel extraction; bound +-20 Pa on every pressure value (assessed by the reader; the authors state none).

column4: Authored flue performance inputs of the alto recorder built from the published geometry and the published register thresholds: network from the tabulated bore, holes and window, the estimated windway height, four held notes at the first-register ceilings and four linear crescendos, the render recipe and the status card
column14: A fixture for listening, not graded: no licensed reference recording exists (bead pexfp.219). Authored items: windway height 1.06 mm (1.8 mm / 1.7 from two other altos; bounds 0.5 to 1.8 mm), flue width = window width, onset ramp 50 ms, jet displacement gain 90, the repository interim slot-jet card, labium offset +0.1455 mm DERIVED from the step and edge (row recorder-labium-offset-bouterse2010-derived) and jet angle zero, hole 7 omitted, the shared exhaled-breath gas pack (row coltman-nederveen-fletcher-woodwind-breath), crescendo ramp 3 to 600 Pa at 100 Pa/s.

column4: Measured planar-jet instability (Schlieren images of CO2 jets at Reynolds about 200, hot-wire profiles at 5, 10 and 20 m/s): convection velocity of the sinuous perturbation c_p / U_j about 0.5 for a short (1 mm) flue channel and about 0.3 for a long (10 mm) channel and for square, rounded and 45-degree exits, nearly constant over Str_h = f h / U_j 0.05 to 1.1; amplification alpha_i h about 0.15 to 0.35 over the same range, peak about 0.35 at Str_h 0.5 to 0.65 (preferred frequencies 0.4 to 0.6), jet stable near Str_h 2; Nolle profile thickness b about 0.45 h to 0.5 h; displacement at the jet origin measured IN PHASE with the acoustic velocity (no pi shift and no 1/omega factor); c_p = 0.3 U_j adopted in the thesis' own model
column14: P. de la Cuadra, The sound of oscillating air jets: physics, modeling and simulation in flute-like instruments, PhD thesis, Stanford University, 2005 (author's CCRMA page; author copyright, facts only). Sec. 2.2.5 to 2.2.8, Fig. 2.14 and 2.17 (values read by eye from plotted points, error about 0.05 in alpha_i h and 0.05 in c_p / U_j), Fig. 2.13, 2.18, and chapter 4 (eq. 4.24 and the text after it). U_j is the CENTRE jet speed. Re about 200 and low flows: the flute's Str_h range (0.01 to 0.04) and Reynolds range (1000 to 2500) are outside these measurements. Chapter 4 text and Fig. 4.11 give the same c_p and alpha_i h for flute-like jets. Reading error (OD17): values read by eye from the plotted points of Fig. 2.14 and Fig. 2.17, no pixel extraction; bound +-0.05 on alpha_i h and +-0.05 on c_p / U_j (assessed by the reader; the thesis states none). Values taken from the thesis text carry the thesis' own rounding.

column4: Linear-response reflection coefficient of the air-jet amplifier of a Yamaha YRT-304B II tenor recorder head (body replaced by a reflectometer, pipe flow blocked): head geometry (bore radius 12.36 mm, windway 72.0 mm long and 14.7 mm wide, 1.95 mm high at the inlet and 1.09 mm at the exit, 45-degree chamfers 0.7 mm deep, lip 4.83 mm from the duct outlet, curved duct radius 2.7 cm); gain band |S_h| > 1 from 223 to 1100 Hz at 250 Pa (St = f W~ / U0 about 0.054 to 0.267, U0 centre speed about 22.8 m/s), a second band below 100 Pa at St 0.43 to 0.60; fitted lumped head inertance equal to a length of 8.9 mm; jet gain 0.145 of the Nolle / Mattingly-Criminale model needed (0.20 with a small pipe flow); playing region bounded by the first band's upper edge
column14: J. C. Price, W. A. Johnston and D. D. McKinnon, Linear-response reflection coefficient of the recorder air-jet amplifier, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 138 (2015) 3282, arXiv 1502.02170 (arXiv non-exclusive licence; facts only). Sec. II geometry, Sec. IV text and Fig. 5, 8 to 12; the band edges are the paper's text; mu b and c_p / U0 of the Bickley jet (Nolle, Mattingly and Criminale) read by eye from Fig. 5 (mu b 0.04 at St_b 0, peak about 0.275 at 0.25, 0 at 1.33; c_p / U0 0.30 at 0, 0.39 at 0.2, 0.5 at 0.6, 0.67 at 1.33; St_b = omega b / U0 with b = 2 h / 5). Used only to test a jet card against a measured response; the head geometry is retained as facts. Reading error (OD17): the gain band edges and the head geometry are the paper's text (stated). The Bickley-jet values mu b and c_p / U0 of Fig. 5 were read by eye at the listed points, no pixel extraction; bound +-0.01 on mu b and +-0.02 on c_p / U0 (assessed by the reader; the paper states none), the same reading as row price-2015-fig5-jet-growth-and-model-constants.

column14: J. C. Price, W. A. Johnston and D. D. McKinnon, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 138 (2015) 3282, arXiv 1502.02170 (arXiv non-exclusive licence; facts only). Fig. 5 (spline fits to the Nolle / Mattingly-Criminale tables at W~/b = 12.7, read by eye at the listed points), Eqs. 4 to 11 and Sec. III and V text. column4: Effective clarinet reed with the embouchure included, inverse-modelled from one performed Bb clarinet excerpt (11 clarion tones): per-tone medians of effective mass 1.68 mg, damping rate 2270.54 1/s, stiffness 1434.15 N/m, equilibrium opening 0.36 mm, tube length 15.59 cm and reed-lay contact stiffness 7.90e6, damping 6.47 s/m and position 0.16 mm; used only as scalar facts on the status card
column14: M. Pamies-Vila, Expressive performance on single-reed woodwind instruments: an experimental characterisation of articulatory actions, PhD thesis, mdw Vienna, 2021, chapter 6 Fig. 6.5 (printed page 102), the same inverse model as Chatziioannou, Schmutzhard, Pamies-Vila and Hofmann, Acta Acustica 105:682, 2019. Reading procedure (owner decision OD17): the eight values used are the numeric labels printed in red beside the median marker of each plot (they are also text in the PDF text layer, which was checked with pdftotext and against a 130 dpi image of PDF page 114): 1.68 mg, 2270.54 s^-1, 1434.15 N/m, 0.36 mm, 15.59 cm, 7.90x10^6 N/m^2 (the exponent is printed in the label), 6.47 s/m and 0.16 mm; no marker position was measured, so the reading error is the printed precision, half of the last printed digit (0.005 in the unit shown for each of the 2-decimal values). The thesis states no uncertainty of the estimate itself, and the per-tone points are not tabulated and are not used. Effective area and width are not printed in the thesis and stay UNKNOWN. An estimate from a player's recording, not a direct measurement of any reed.

column4: Human vocal fold cover and ligament, measured separately per subject: longitudinal modulus from cyclic tension with optical strain, transverse modulus and longitudinal shear modulus from inverse analysis of transverse indentation
column14: Kelleher, Siegmund, Du, Naseri, Chan, Biomech. Model. Mechanobiol. 12:555-567; PMC3745772 author manuscript read as text; Tables 1 and 2 and the Results sentences. Six subjects (3 male, 3 female, 45-97 y, 18-76 h postmortem), one cover and one contralateral ligament specimen each. All at 1 Hz, far below the phonatory rate; geriatric donors; preliminary by the authors' own statement. E_T and G_L are strongly coupled inverse estimates (10 percent on G_L moves E_T by 30 percent). Test temperature not stated. Per-value uncertainty not printed. Numeric facts only; the table layout is not reproduced. Muscle (thyroarytenoid) layer not in this source.

column4: Human true and false vocal fold longitudinal and transverse Young's modulus, longitudinal shear modulus, Poisson ratio and a measured tissue density
column14: Alipour and Vigmostad, J. Voice 26(6):816.e21-816.e29; PMC3508138 author manuscript read as text; Table 1 and the Methods and Results sentences. Cadaveric larynges of donors aged 53-82 y, quick-frozen and stored 3-4 y, thawed overnight; 1 Hz cyclic loading; mean and standard deviation over N=5 to 10 samples per quantity. Includes the first MEASURED human fold tissue density in the ledger (Archimedes, N=10, g/mL converted to kg/m3), which supersedes the stated-constant register note of tissue-density-titze-2016 for measured use. Strongly nonlinear tissue: a single modulus is a low-strain tangent. Numeric facts only; the table layout is not reproduced.

column4: Human vocal fold effective Young's modulus by indentation of intact hemilarynx, isolated cover (superior, medial, inferior medial) and isolated thyroarytenoid muscle, with indenter and sample geometry per row
column14: Chhetri, Zhang, Neubauer, J. Voice 25(1):1-7; PMC2891297 author manuscript read as text; Tables 1-3 and Results. Three larynges (male 49 y, female 19 y, male 30 y), autopsy within 48 h, quick-frozen at -80 C. APPARATUS RESPONSE: an effective indentation modulus of thin samples, not a constitutive constant; the authors' silicone-rubber calibration shows overestimation when depth exceeds the indenter diameter, so h/D and D/T of every row are carried as validity. Per-row spread is an interquartile range of five unloading curves (a full width). The printed TA muscle range 1.3-2.7 kPa does not contain the Table 3 value 3.1 kPa (an inconsistency in the source, recorded). This is the only thyroarytenoid muscle stiffness in the ledger; transverse direction only, quasi-static. Layer thicknesses stated in the Introduction (TA about 6 mm, lamina propria about 2 mm, epithelium 0.1-0.2 mm) are geometry, not material data: they are NOT in the pack (bead rule) and are recorded here only. Marked per the bead: properties end _apparatus_effective, observations start apparatus-, never resolvable as an intrinsic modulus.

column4: Measured, reverse-engineered construction plan of a 1964 Madrid classical-type guitar (plan header: Sobrinos de Domingo Esteso, scale length 650 mm): printed dimensions, brace and bar widths and heights, bridge, neck, headstock, lining and rib numbers, woods; the top and side views are plotted 1:1

File 1_construction_plan.pdf, 2549696 bytes, sha256 63f26c85fbfb7ce74454e587941927972c4e4c75fd086ae490f4bc1169e4f745; drawing and measurement by Stefan Zimmer, 2024. IDENTITY DISCREPANCY recorded, not resolved: the record title names Faustino Conde (flamenca negra, 1964); the plan header and label photograph say Sobrinos de Domingo Esteso, Madrid, Gravina 7, 1964. Table I and a mobility figure are printed on the plan with no stated origin (the record cites Mores 2021, JASA 149(2) 1041); the figure is not transcribed.

column4: Positions of the printed thickness values (top 54 points, back 55, ribs 9) and of the other printed numeric labels of the same plan, read from the text layer of the PDF and converted to millimetres
column14: The thickness VALUES are the author's printed numbers (text); what is read from the drawing is each value's POSITION: the centre of the printed label, assumed to sit at the author's measurement circle, in PDF points from the plan's text layer, converted at 72/25.4 pt per mm for the top and side views (plotted 1:1: the vector outline height 1040.4 pt = 367.03 mm against the printed 367,02, a 0.003 percent check) and at 812.9 pt / 495 mm = 1.6422 pt/mm for the back view (scale from the printed overall length; the vector outline height gives 367.7 mm against 367.03, 0.2 percent). Reading error bounded by 1 mm (top, side) and 2 mm (back), plus the author's own placement accuracy and gauge precision, which are not stated (u-position-reading, u-thickness-between-points). Values are taken only when the horizontal label is d,d or d.d between 1.3 and 3.0, not preceded by an h: label; the count was cross-checked against the circles visible in the drawing. printed-annotations.tsv lists every other numeric label with view, orientation and position and assigns none to a feature.

column4: Measured signature modes of the same guitar as printed in Table I on the plan: A0 98 Hz, T1 200, T2 240, T3 277, T4 317 and A1 408 Hz with the author's descriptions (relevant to M8-W8f; this is not a bridge admittance)

The frequency uncertainty, the measurement method and the excitation are not stated on the plan; the figure printed beside the table (a mobility curve) is not transcribed. The plan does not state the origin of the table; the record cites Mores 2021, JASA 149(2) 1041, as the associated article.

column4: Archive of acoustical documentation (bridge mobility plots, raw impulse data qualified_selected_impulses.mat, MATLAB scripts, List_of_guitars_physical_measures.pdf, photographs) of more than 60 classical, flamenco and romantic Spanish guitars; whether the Esteso 1964 guitar is included is not confirmed

Conde guitars are among the files (g14, g20, g40); the Esteso 1964 guitar is not confirmed. The mobility plots are figures (digitization frozen); the raw .mat impulses and the physical-measures PDF would be the usable parts if the licence allows. Source for the next step toward M8-W8f for classical guitars.

column4: Outline curves, sound hole circle and fret lines of the same plan read from the PDF's vector paths: the top outline (486 points), a second open thick path (209) that completes the outline as the treble upper bout (its far end lies 0.33 mm from the first point of the first path; the outline stays open by 60.19 mm at the neck end, the printed neck width), the sound hole circle (33), the back outline (570, scale from the printed 495 mm) and 14 candidate fret lines
column14: Method: the plan is an exact AutoCAD vector plot (svg from pdftocairo, path units x 0.03 = PDF points, 1 mm = 72/25.4 pt), so a path coordinate is read to 0.01 mm of the plot; no raster was traced. Checks against the author's printed numbers: vector height of the top outline 367.02 mm against the printed 367,02; vector sound hole circle diameter 87.01 mm against the printed R43,5 (x 106.19..193.20 mm, y -43.79..43.22 mm; centre 149.70 mm from the outline's extreme point against the printed 151 from a datum the author does not define: a 1.3 mm unexplained difference); the back view's y extent 367.73 mm against 367.02 mm at the scale set by the printed 495 mm (0.2 percent). Reading error bounded by 0.1 mm against the plot for the 1:1 views and by 1 mm (0.2 percent of 495 mm) for the back view; the drafting accuracy of the author is not stated and is not included. Fret lines: ten fret lines and the nut line coincide with equal temperament for a 650 mm scale to within 0.03 mm, one line (the sixth) is 6.3 mm short and the tenth is not drawn; this agreement is tighter than measuring a real fingerboard gives, so the lines were most likely constructed, and the real guitar's frets are NOT thereby measured (unknowns.tsv u-fret-positions). Not read: brace outlines (drawn as thousands of short dashed segments), dimension geometry, photographs.

column4: Top bracing of the same plan read from the dashed hidden-line vectors: 35 straight dashed lines and the 12 brace strips (11 bars) they pair into, with measured widths, centre lines and the printed width and h: labels assigned to them
column14: Method: the hidden brace edges are drawn as dashes of 5.67 pt with 2.8 pt gaps in the exact vector plot; 2578 dash segments of the front view were chained into 35 straight dashed lines (facing ends within 3.4 pt, direction within 3 degrees, lateral offset under 0.6 pt) and parallel lines 4 to 14 mm apart were paired into strips. Check against the author's printed numbers, made after the pairing and not used in it: the 12 measured strip widths are 7.00, 10.96, 7.00, 7.00, 11.01, 5.00, 8.50, 8.50, 13.00, 8.50, 5.00 and 8.00 mm and every one equals a printed width (5, 7, 8, 8.5, 11, 13) to 0.05 mm. The printed h: labels are assigned to strips by P7 from the label position and the arrow target seen on the drawing, not from the arrow vectors (the assignments are in the note column; h: 2,0 and h: 0,7 at the bridge position and h: 4,0 at the annulus around the hole stay unassigned). Reading error: coordinates to 0.01 mm of the plot; line end points are the outer ends of the visible dashed run and are uncertain by up to one dash period (about 3 mm) and by tapered or hidden bar ends; bounded 0.1 mm across a strip and 3 mm along it. The drafting accuracy of the author is not stated and not included. Seven dashed edges stay unpaired (short pieces, not bars); cross-section shapes are not read (unknowns.tsv).

column4: Human vocal fold cover linear viscoelastic shear moduli G', G'' and dynamic viscosity at phonatory frequencies 1-250 Hz: power-law fits to the mean of seven specimens, with the mean loss factor over 100-250 Hz
column14: Chan and Rodriguez, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 124(2):1207-1219; PMC2561277 author manuscript read as text; Tables 1 and 2 and the Results sentences. Simple-shear rheometer, 1.0 mm gap, 1.0 percent shear strain, chamber about 37 C and near 100 percent RH; seven covers (53-88 y; five cadaveric within 20 h, two total laryngectomy). Fits are to the MEAN of seven specimens, valid inside 1-250 Hz only; G'' exceeds G' below about 50 Hz. The source's damping ratio is the loss factor G''/G'; mean 0.7383 +- 0.1211 over 100-250 Hz, against the 0.1-0.2 of fold models. Standard deviations of the moduli are printed only in a figure and are not recorded. Four derived evaluations (G' and G'' at 100 and 250 Hz) are computed here from the printed fits and labelled as such. Numeric facts only; the table layout is not reproduced.

column4: Monofilament nylon, fluorocarbon and natural gut instrument strings: kHz storage modulus (a straight line in stress for nylon and fluorocarbon, fixed for gut), constant loss modulus, loss factor and bulk density
column14: Woodhouse and Lynch-Aird, Acta Acustica 105:516-529 (2019), Table I and Eqs. 16-17, read in the article text by P2. Commercial strings of unknown composition; temperature and humidity of the underlying measurements are not stated in this paper (the same authors' 2018 temperature and humidity results were withdrawn by their 2023 corrigendum and are not used); the stress range of the E' fit is not printed as numbers. A design-chart fit, not a constitutive law.

column4: Violin bow force, bow velocity and hair tension from a frog-end force sensor with motion-capture bow position: typical force 0.5 to 1.5 N in normal playing, reconstruction error about 0.05 N for slow variations between 0.5 and 2 N; one player's detache about 0.6 N at 30 to 60 cm/s (G4 on the D string), accented strokes up to 2 N at about 80 cm/s with softer parts about 0.5 N at 20 cm/s, a two-sensor example about 1.2 N at about 30 cm/s; the authors' bow: transverse tip stiffness 91 N/m, hair length 0.53 m, fitted hair tension 50.2 N (inputs of the bowed-string player: force and velocity ranges, never fit targets)
column14: M. Demoucron, A. Askenfelt and R. Causse, Measuring bow force in bowed string performance: theory and implementation of a bow force sensor, Acta Acustica united with Acustica 95(4) 2009 pp.718-732; read in the author's HAL copy https://hal.science/hal-00444903/document (HAL authorization, publisher copyright, not retained). Text values only, each with its section in the table's locator column; the traces of Figs. 18 and 20 are figures and are not retained. Two violinists were asked to play detache and accented strokes; which player made which example is not stated. The force is the transverse force at the end of the hair at the frog plus the bow position (motion capture, or a second sensor at the tip), so it is a reconstruction: its stated error is about 0.05 N for slow variations between 0.5 and 2 N and larger for very stiff bows at low force (3 percent per 1 percent sensor error for one bow, 15 percent for a carbon-fibre one at 0.5 to 1 N); tilting the bow changes the calibration by more than 30 percent near the sensor. The row 0.5 to 1.5 N is the authors' calibration choice and quotes Askenfelt 1986. A player force is an input to a physical model, never a fit target.

column4: Violin bow force in short bow strokes: sautille maximum force 0.74 N in one mf example at 90 bpm and fitted maxima from about 0.5 N in piano to more than 3 N in forte across p, mf and f at 90 and 150 bpm; fast martele force falling from about 1.5 N to under 0.5 N within a stroke with a 13 Hz stick ripple (inputs of the short-stroke player model)
column14: M. Demoucron, The violinist's bestiary: characterizing bowing parameters of technical bow strokes, Proc. 2nd Vienna Talk, Vienna 2010, pp.55-58; no licence is printed; text values only. The per-dynamic and per-tempo values of the fitted force maximum and velocity amplitude (Fig. 4) and the traces (Figs. 1 and 5) are figures and are not retained; the stroke models (two cosines for the force pulse, a half sine for the velocity, a sine decrease after a pinch for martele) are functional forms, and the fitted parameter values are in the author's thesis (KTH 2008, not retrieved). The player, the violin and the calibration are not stated in this paper, which refers to Schoonderwaldt and Demoucron (J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 126(5) 2009) for the measuring system, so no error bound is available. A player force is an input to a physical model, never a fit target.

column4: Second-hand values from Askenfelt's two violinists: bow force variation within a stroke under 0.2 N in piano and under 0.7 N in forte; player 1 piano 29 cm/s, 42 mm from the bridge, 0.5 N and forte 21 cm/s, 18 mm, 2.3 N; player 2 piano 21 cm/s, 42 mm, 0.4 N and forte 24 cm/s, 20 mm, 1.7 N; dynamic difference about 9 dB; gravity changes the force at the frog by about 3 N for a normal violin bow along a horizontal path (inputs of the bowed-string player: dynamics made by position and force rather than speed)
column14: K. Guettler, A closer look at the string player's bowing gestures, Catgut Acoustical Society Journal Vol. 4 No. 7 (Series II), May 2003, author-hosted on knutsacoustics.com, no licence printed; text values only. SECOND-HAND: every number is Guettler's quotation or summary of Askenfelt, Measurement of the bowing parameters in violin playing II, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 86(2) 1989 pp.503-516, which is closed and was not read, so the transcription follows Guettler's wording and cannot be checked against the original here. Two violinists on one violin and one adapted bow (as described by Chudy, Dixon and Perez, ICA 2013). The bow-to-bridge distance is in mm, not the ratio beta, and the string length is not stated in the passage. No measurement uncertainty is stated in the quoted passages. A player value is an input to a physical model, never a fit target.

column4: Cello bow position, bow velocity and relative bow-bridge distance of one professional cellist playing the cello part of Vivaldi's Spring on the open strings A3, D3 and G2 (68 s at 240 frames per s), derived by script from the open motion-capture markers: bow position 13 to 49 cm from the frog, median absolute bow velocity 21 cm/s (maximum 91 cm/s), bow-bridge distance over string length 0.086 to 0.122 (5th to 95th percentile), bow-to-string angle 83 to 90 degrees (inputs of the cello bowing player model; no force)
column14: M. Pamies-Vila, A. Mayer, E. Matusiak and V. Chatziioannou, dataset of 'A method for the reproduction of cello bow kinematics using a robotic arm and motion capture', Acta Acustica 2024, Zenodo, CC BY 4.0, recorded at mdw Vienna in February 2023 with OptiTrack Prime 13 at 240 fps. Machine-read from the open data file DataMocap_Player.csv (md5 7cc2513edfc033108700a3fab3f35dce as on the Zenodo record, sha-256 2dcf299ca572a84ef3a3103ce5065602ada5b2e9e1f337ac57a3bc6055f29f1c, not committed) by data/instruments/descriptions/players/derive_cello_bow_kinematics.py; not hand-transcribed. The derived table has 16323 rows (frame index = time x 240) and the script has a synthetic-rig test. Bow axis = MFrog to MTip, string = MNut to MBridge; their closest approach gives the position, the velocity (central differences, relative to the string line), the ratio of the contact-to-bridge distance to the nut-bridge marker distance (0.695 m), the line separation and the skew. LIMITS: the file has no force and no contact signal; the markers are on the ends of the stick, not on the hair, so whether the hair is on the string CANNOT be read from the kinematics (the line separation is 20 to 74 mm from the 5th to the 95th percentile); the bridge marker sits on top of the bridge, so the ratio carries that offset; one professional player, open strings only, a slow piece; marker accuracy is not stated in the files read. The two robot recordings and the audio of the record were not downloaded. A player motion is an input to a physical model, never a fit target.

column4: Violin motion capture of 11 amateur violinists imitating an avatar's bowings in orchestral excerpts (Dvorak 8, Holst Mars, Brahms 2): Qualisys 120 Hz, three markers on the bow and three or four on the violin, a 2.6 GB labelled file set and audio at 48 kHz; bow velocity and bow-bridge distance are not yet derivable (acquisition open)
column14: A. Campo, A. Michalko, B. Van Kerrebroeck and M. Leman, dataset for the assessment of presence and performance in an augmented reality environment for motor imitation learning (violinists), Zenodo 2023, CC BY 4.0; article PMC10587485. Players: 11 student-orchestra violinists with at least 12 years of violin (mean 14.7). Read: the record, the article through a summarising fetch, one AnalyzedData file (columns PD, dSI, startIndex, endIndex, per-note rows, meanings not stated in what was read, no bow column) and the header of one labelled-mocap member (P006_T1_2D_F1, 21839 frames) by range request. The bow markers are named BOW_P008 - 1 to 3 and the violin markers VIOLIN_P006 - 1 to 3 (the participant number in the bow name does not match the file name), with no stated placement relative to the frog, tip, bridge or nut, so a bow axis, a string line and thereby bow velocity and bow-bridge distance cannot be computed without the paper's marker figure or the authors' calibration. The article is said to include bow-to-bridge distance and tilt in derived files; not confirmed. Open: obtain the marker placement (the paper's figure, or the authors through the owner if a request is needed), then derive as for the cello. No force. Amateurs and orchestral excerpts, not a controlled note-by-note design.

column4: Horse bow-hair: static Young's modulus 7 +- 0.5 GPa and dynamic 9 +- 1.5 GPa at 10 to 100 Hz (the paper states +-15 % on the dynamic data), loss factor of the order of 0.02 to 0.05, density about 1100 kg/m^3, diameter 0.16 to 0.25 mm, and Table I ribbon hair counts, masses, lengths and widths for violin, viola, cello and double-bass bows
column14: Pitteroff and Woodhouse, Acustica - acta acustica 84:543-562 (1998), pp. 545-549 read on page images by P2 (P6's hunt file lists the same numbers). Pack matdb:bow-hair-horse-pitteroff-woodhouse-acustica1998 (its manifest says permitted, the only term the pack compiler accepts; this row's true term is facts-only, so the row does not link it). Hair origin, humidity and temperature are not stated; the 2500 m/s +-3 % wave speed is Schumacher's, quoted; hair counts are estimates from the mass of commercial hanks.

column4: Rosin: density 1010 kg/m^3, thermal conductivity 0.113 W/m/K and specific heat 250 J/kg/K (simulation inputs; the conductivity and specific heat are Cobbold and Jackson 1992 and the paper calls the specific heat unexpectedly low) and the viscosity law eta = 3000 x 10^((50 - T)/10) Pa s, T in kelvin above 20 C, fitted to 100 rad/s rheometer data over 45 to 85 C
column14: Smith and Woodhouse, J. Mech. Phys. Solids 48:1633-1681 (2000), Table 1, Section 4.1 and Eq. (3) read on the publisher PDF (Eq. (3) on a page image) by P2. Pack matdb:rosin-smith-woodhouse-jmps2000 (not linked: see the bow-hair row). The rosin's brand and grade are not stated; no glass transition temperature is printed in this paper; the paper's own Fig. 12 caption cites the fit as Eq. (1).

column4: Violin rosin glass transition: calorimetry measurements suggest a transition temperature around 50 C
column14: Woodhouse and Galluzzo, Tribology Letters (2025), the Cambridge repository accepted version (handle 1810/388990), whose record states CC BY 4.0; Section 2, one sentence read by P2. Brand, formulation and heating rate are not stated; the paper says commercial formulations differ.

column4: Rosin glass transition temperatures by differential scanning calorimetry: 49 C for a violin rosin and 16 C for a double-bass rosin
column14: Woodhouse, Euphonics section 9.6, Figure 11 caption and the paragraph below it, read by P2. The site's content is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 except where noted, so only the two numbers are retained as facts. Pack matdb:rosin-glass-transition-woodhouse-euphonics-9-6 (not linked: see the bow-hair row). Brands and heating rate are not stated.

column4: Missing measured multifilament string cores (nylon, Perlon, silk, synthetic), silver-plated copper and other winding wires and winding alloys: density, modulus and loss against frequency, temperature and humidity
column14: P2 winding hunt (2026-10-21, 90 min, a literature agent plus P2's reading of the best leads): still NOT found in any readable source: density, Young's modulus and loss factor of a named commercial multifilament nylon, Perlon or silk core measured on the core alone; density, modulus, hardness and loss of silver, aluminium, chrome-steel or silver-plated-copper winding wire as drawn; any humidity or temperature dependence of a core or winding; measured torsional damping of a wound string. FOUND and landed (Firth 1987 construction of 16 violin strings: core, underwrap and wrap wire diameters, silver or aluminium, in the row firth-1987-violin-string-construction): whole wound cello strings with measured bending stiffness (Lampis 2024), the core-against-string weight split of commercial gut and nylon violin strings and a PVDF core's modulus (Kureha patent), the modulus range a nylon 6 core was specified to have (Behringer patent), torsional stiffness and resonances of a steel-cored wound bass string (Bavu 2005), measured winding and core densities of commercial guitar strings (Parker patent). Earlier note: whole-string data also exist in Pickering 1985 and 1986 (scanned, no licence stated; the 1985 table is in violin-strings-whole-pickering-jcas1985). Sources named but not reachable: Bell and Firth 1986 (Acustica 60:87-89), Chaigne (CAS J. 1:21-27, 1991), Wollman, Smith and Wolfe (ISMA 2010, UNSW server unreachable), the Cambridge string test reports (200-330 page PDFs, not read).

column4: Unstretched diameter and bulk density of 14 harp strings: Bowbrand nylon 1072 to 1159 kg/m^3 in two density groups (the thicker strings higher), Savarez fluorocarbon 1729 to 1819 (monofilament above wound), Bowbrand gut 1320 to 1325
column14: Lynch-Aird and Woodhouse, Materials 11(11):2160 (2018), Table 1 only, read in the PubMed Central text by P2 (diameters by manual micrometer, 0.01 mm resolution; densities measured before testing). The same authors' 2023 paper says the whole of Section 4 here (temperature and humidity behaviour of gut) rests on erroneous load-cell data and must be ignored, and that the load-cell characterisation was faulty at low temperature: nothing from those parts is in this pack.

column4: Natural gut harp strings with twist angle 23.5 to 58.3 degrees and diameter 1.328 to 1.990 mm: unstretched bulk density 1283 to 1329 kg/m^3, stretched density settling at 97 to 98 percent of the unstretched value, breaking strain typically 0.15 to 0.28
column14: Lynch-Aird and Woodhouse, Materials 16(15):5444 (2023), Table 1 extremes and statements of Sections 3.1-3.2 read in the PubMed Central text by P2: the ranges, not the 25 section rows. Breaking stress against twist angle is figure-only and is not in the pack; the authors estimate breaking stress on the actual diameter would be around 10 to 15 percent higher. Humidity sensitivity of gut is not captured.

column4: Thirty-five violin strings (Dominant, Super Sensitive, Jargar, Corelli, Kaplan, Gold Label, Eudoxa; gut, Perlon, synthetic, steel and silver-wound constructions): relaxed diameter and length, tension at the open pitch, wave impedance, linear mass, torsional stiffness, torsional damping coefficient and overtone tuning in cents (table on p. 7)
column14: Pickering, J. Catgut Acoust. Soc. 44:6-8 (Nov 1985): the dot-matrix table read twice on 320 dpi page images by P2, with the table's own identities as the check: sqrt(tension x linear mass) equals the printed wave impedance in all 35 rows (largest deviation 0.22 percent, the Gold Label G row) and tension equals linear mass x (2 L f)^2 for the 329 mm test-bed length at the open-string frequency to within -0.79 to -0.54 percent. The Kaplan A(5) and Gold Label A rows print identical tension, impedance and mass (kept as printed). The scan states no licence and its host cautions about copyright; humidity and temperature are not stated; the units of the torsional stiffness (g-cm per rad) and of the damping coefficient are the table's own. Pack matdb:violin-strings-whole-pickering-jcas1985 (not linked: this row is facts-only). Whole-string values only: no core density, modulus or winding loss.

column4: Shell-ready orthotropic constants of Sitka spruce and western redcedar (density, E_L, E_R, nu_LR, G_LR, G_LT, G_RT) computed by arithmetic from the Wood Handbook bending MOE, specific gravity and elastic ratios already retained in the seed packs, with the nine Kelvin-Voigt viscosities built from measured directional loss factors (Qiu et al. 2026 Sitka eta_L; Bremaud, Gril and Thibaut 2011 Table 4 directional ratios)
column14: Derived rows only: E_L is 1.10 times the printed bending MOE (the chapter's shear-deflection correction), E_R, G_LR, G_LT, G_RT are the Table 5-1 ratios times E_L, density is 1000 x SG x 1.12. Sitka spruce is NOT the species of the Esteso 1964 top (the plan says spruce only) and western redcedar is NOT the plan's cedar (species unnamed); both are the Wood Handbook species with a full elastic set. Static handbook values are used at audio frequency; the omega validity band of the packs is declared by the pack author. Loss: spruce eta_L is the mean of the two Qiu et al. Sitka beam values (0.01424 at 62 Hz, 0.01134 at about 830 Hz) with the resonance-spruce directional ratios of Bremaud et al.; cedar uses the Bremaud softwood row as a SURROGATE; viscosities are eta x stiffness / omega_ref with omega_ref = 2 pi 200 rad/s, a Kelvin-Voigt law whose loss factor grows with frequency: a consumer must rescale per mode by omega_ref/omega. The packs also carry five dimensionless loss_factor_1, loss_factor_2, loss_factor_12, loss_factor_13 and loss_factor_23 scalars in the material axes (valid 2 pi 50 to 2 pi 1000 rad/s, a band declared by the pack author) for the constant-loss-factor shell path, with the same sources, and the Poisson cross term of the viscosities uses the arithmetic mean of the two in-plane loss factors (Adams-Bacon split), so the two realisations agree on every entry.

column4: Shell-ready constants for Brazilian rosewood (Rio rosewood of the plan's back and sides): E_L and density from the Wood Handbook (density through the Handbook's own shrinkage rule), E_R, G_LR and G_LT from the African padauk anisotropy ratios of Bremaud, Gril and Thibaut 2011 Table 4, G_RT and nu_LR as the mean of six Wood Handbook hardwoods; viscosities explicit zero
column14: SURROGATE pack: the Wood Handbook prints no elastic ratios for any rosewood, so E_R, G_LR and G_LT use padauk ratios (E_L/E_R = 7, E_L/G_LR = 9, E_L/G_LT = 9.7; the table marks part of that row as adjusted values) because the same paper reports that padauk parameters predict the measured grain-angle dependence of Rio rosewood; G_RT (0.0198 E_L) and nu_LR (0.3625) are means over yellow birch, African and Honduras mahogany, sweetgum, black walnut and yellow-poplar. Density 944 kg/m3 is 1000 x 0.80 x 1.12 / (1 - 0.085 x 18/30) from Table 5-5a (green-volume SG basis) and Table 4-3b volumetric shrinkage 8.5 percent. Every result built on this pack must report its sensitivity to these choices. Loss: padauk eta_L 0.0048 with its directional ratios (R 3.1, LR 2.1, LT 2.13), a LOW surrogate value (a dynamic-mechanical test of Dalbergia nigra elsewhere gives tan delta 0.022 under other conditions); viscosities are eta x stiffness / omega_ref with omega_ref = 2 pi 200 rad/s. The packs also carry five dimensionless loss_factor_1, loss_factor_2, loss_factor_12, loss_factor_13 and loss_factor_23 scalars in the material axes (valid 2 pi 50 to 2 pi 1000 rad/s, a band declared by the pack author) for the constant-loss-factor shell path, with the same sources, and the Poisson cross term of the viscosities uses the arithmetic mean of the two in-plane loss factors (Adams-Bacon split), so the two realisations agree on every entry.

column4: Closed-body shell assembly of the Esteso 1964 guitar at a 12 mm target edge length: top with sound hole, 11 brace walls, back with 4 ladder bars, two rib strips and the tie lists between them, with the cavity volume and neck derived from them; built from the retained plan tables by the generator in crates/fs-couple/examples/guitar_body_modes/
column14: Derived mesh of the vector reads in the plan-vector and plan-braces rows (their reading errors apply) plus AUTHORED choices written as meta rows in the file itself: uniform thickness per component as the cube root of the mean cube of the printed points (top 2.468, back 2.312, ribs 1.631 mm), back surface as the quadratic through the three printed rib depths with no cross arch, brace walls as full-length rectangles of printed width and height (cross-section shape, taper and crossings UNKNOWN), straight transverse back bars at the printed 91 mm and mean printed spacings, the two dashed runs of the slanted bar bridged into one, the back view outline replaced by the top outline. NOT modelled: bridge, neck and heel, tail and heel blocks, linings, rosette, fingerboard, strings, the central back strip and patches. The outline is the first path, the second path (treble upper bout) and a straight 60.19 mm neck-end closure. Cavity volume is not printed on the plan; the file value (13.0 L) comes from the facets. Rib and ladder-bar nodes sit exactly on the tied skins (worst tie gap about 1e-9 m); the first version of this table placed them with a vertical offset under the tilted back (64 micrometre gap), which made the assembled mass matrix lose positive definiteness in the shell owner, and was replaced. column4: HARP, NOT GUITAR: contact-mechanics prior only, never a guitar gesture. Finger-on-string release of ten harpists (six professionals H1 to H6, four amateurs H7 to H10) plucking one gut string of a concert harp (30th string, Db2, 138.6 Hz, 260 N, 97.5 cm, 1.96 mm) with the right forefinger and annular finger in chords and arpeggios at mezzo-forte, filmed at the string by a high-speed camera: sticking-phase duration 56 to 431 ms and slipping-phase duration 1.2 to 6.1 ms per player and context (each with its 95 percent interval), maximum rotation of the string by the finger during sticking 11 to 82 degrees, initial angle of attack of the released string 7 to 44 degrees, release displacement about 4 mm and release velocity about 2 m/s on average (extremes 0.5 to 7 mm and 0.2 to 5 m/s), a computed peak finger force up to 15 N, plucking position one third to two fifths of the string length, finger width on the string about 2 cm (a population prior for the trajectory, timing and release conditions of a fingertip release; inputs of a plucked-string excitation model, never fit targets)
column14: D. Chadefaux, J.-L. Le Carrou, B. Fabre and L. Daudet, Experimentally based description of harp plucking, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 131(1) 2012 pp.844-855; read in the authors' copy https://www.lam.jussieu.fr/Publications/Articles/JASA_Chadefaux_2012.pdf (ASA copyright, not retained). Tables I to VI and the text values are hand-transcribed from the printed tables (page images read cell by cell next to the text layer; empty cells stay empty: 37, 37, 32 and 36 cells in Tables II, III, IV and VI); every row of the table file carries the label 'harp, not guitar: contact-mechanics prior only, never a guitar gesture'. Errors: each cell of Tables II to IV and VI has its printed 95 percent half-width; the event instants have about three frames (0.58 ms); the text states about 10 percent (II, III), 19 percent (IV) and 15 percent (VI). THE PAPER DISAGREES WITH ITSELF in three small places, kept as printed and flagged in the row notes: the text gives 7 to 82 degrees for Table IV whose smallest cell is 11; the text gives 7 to 43 degrees for Table VI whose largest cells are 44; the printed finger averages 44 and 45 degrees do not reproduce from the Table IV cells (43.1 and 41.8) although the chord and arpeggio averages 39 and 45 do. Figs. 7 (plucking position per harpist) and 8 (release displacement and velocity per player with intervals) are figures and are not read; they could be added under OD17 with a stated read error. LIMITS: one string, the right hand only, one harp, ten players of whom four are amateurs, plucking position imposed by the marker spacing, one dynamic (mezzo-forte chords at 60 bpm, arpeggios at 120 bpm); the force is computed from the string trajectory by classical plucked-string theory, not measured; the paper measures no pad compliance, friction coefficient or nail state; a guitar pluck differs (nylon strings, different tension and diameter, nail use, plucking position), so none of these values is a guitar gesture. A player value is an input to a physical model, never a fit target.

column4: The open area of a trombonist's vibrating lips against the MEAN height of the opening (averaged over its width, not the maximum height), from front-view high-speed video through a transparent mouthpiece of five trombonists and an artificial mouth: the power law S = S_o (h/h_o)^q, the time-averaged lip separation h_0 per note and dynamic (five-player means, Bb1 ff 2.0 mm down to D4 mf 0.3 mm), q of player AJ per note and dynamic (0.95 to 2.4, rising with pitch and falling with level), q 'from just below 1 to over 2' across the five players and 1.3 to 1.6 for the artificial mouth, q about 2 or more while opening and about 1 mid-cycle, and the stated accuracies (0.2 mm, 1 mm^2) (the lip-aperture law of a one-degree-of-freedom lip model: a lip pressed to a mouthpiece rim seen from the front, not a tissue property)
column14: S. Bromage, M. Campbell and J. Gilbert, Open areas of vibrating lips in trombone playing, Acta Acustica united with Acustica 96(4) 2010 pp.603-613; read in the HAL preprint hal-00474644 (submitted 21 Apr 2010, HAL authorization, publisher copyright, no Creative Commons licence), so the numbers are the preprint's and the print may differ. Tables 1 and 2 and the text values are hand-transcribed, each with its section in the table file. h is the MEAN height of the opening averaged over the width of the opening, not the maximum height (the paper adopts it because the mean gives a more regular curve); q is the slope of a log-log plot of S against h; S_o is NOT tabulated. Only player AJ's q is tabulated (the paper calls AJ typical); the single q holds only for h above 0.25 mm at p and above 0.6 mm at mf and ff, below which the smallest openings follow a different law; q is not constant within a cycle (opening and closing about 2 or above, mid-cycle about 1 where the width is constant) and some low loud notes show hysteresis, so one q is a fit, not a law of the lips. Conditions: five amateur or semi-professional trombonists (four named by initials), King tenor trombone, transparent perspex mouthpiece with a Denis Wick 6BS rim and a 12 ml cup (larger than the reference mouthpiece, so a lower low-frequency impedance peak), Phantom v4.1 at typically 5000 frames per s, liquid soap on the window; only the 2-D projection is analysed. Stated errors: threshold +-1 pixel = +-0.06 to +-0.121 mm, pixel conversion 2 %, linear measures to 0.2 mm, areas to 1 mm^2, h below 0.2 mm excluded; no confidence interval on q (one range, 1.5 to 2.5, for F4 mf). The figure-versus-table conflict at F4 mf is kept as printed in the Fig. 17 row. Not read and open: Bromage's 2007 thesis (Edinburgh ERA hdl 1842/1966) and Stevenson's 2009 thesis (hdl 1842/4349). APPARATUS-EFFECTIVE like every lip value here: it describes a lip loaded by a mouthpiece, never a tissue modulus.

column4: The area-height exponent q against playing frequency read by eye from Fig. 17 of Bromage, Campbell and Gilbert 2010 under OD17 with a stated read error of +-0.1 in q: player AJ mf about 1.2, 1.3, 1.6, 2.0 at Bb1, Bb2, F3, F4 and p about 1.8, 1.7, 1.8, 2.4; the artificial mouth mf about 1.3 (near 110 Hz) and 1.6 (near 165 Hz) and p about 1.5 (near 165 Hz); the figure's F4 mf value (about 2.0) DISAGREES with Table 2's 1.9 and both are kept as printed

Gilbert, Open areas of vibrating lips in trombone playing, Acta Acustica united with Acustica 96(4) 2010 pp.603-613, Fig. 17 on the last page of the HAL preprint hal-00474644, read by eye from a 110 dpi render against the gridlines (no digitizing software): q read to +-0.1 (my estimate), the artificial mouth's frequencies to +-10 Hz; AJ's x positions are taken as the equal-tempered frequencies of the notes (58.27, 116.54, 174.61, 349.23 Hz, my arithmetic from the note names), where the markers sit to the resolution of the plot. The AJ values agree with the printed Table 2 within the read error EXCEPT F4 mf (figure about 2.0, Table 2 prints 1.9 with range 1.5-2.5): not resolved, both kept. The artificial mouth's 165 Hz points are E3, whose printed text values are 1.49 (85 dB) and 1.55 (103 dB), consistent with 1.5 (p) and 1.6 (mf) read here. h is the width-averaged mean height, as in the main row bromage-2010-lip-open-area-height-law.
