column4: Mechanical response of human trombone lips formed into an embouchure, measured by high-speed video while a calibrated loudspeaker sine sweep drives them through a double-shanked mouthpiece (four semi-professional players, Bb1, Bb2, F3): every curve has one dominant outward-striking resonance below the played note (32 Hz for the Bb1 pedal note played at 58 Hz), a weaker inward-striking resonance above it (74 Hz for Bb1), Q of the lower resonances 1.2 to 1.8 against 8 to 10 for artificial lips (human Q 10 to 20 percent of artificial), and video against laser agreement within 5 percent on artificial lips (an apparatus-effective two-resonance lip: lip plus mouthpiece cavity, not a tissue property)
column14: M. J. Newton, M. Campbell and J. Gilbert, Mechanical response measurements of real and artificial brass players lips, J. Acoust. Soc. Am. 123(1) 2008 pp.EL14-EL20 (online 13 Dec 2007); read in Edinburgh Research Explorer's publisher PDF (ASA copyright, no Creative Commons licence; also HAL hal-00474652). Text values only, with their sections in the table file; the per-note, per-player curves are Fig. 4 and were not read, and Newton's thesis (already in the ledger as newton-2009-thesis-human-lip-mechanical-response) holds the per-player numbers. The video method: 2 kHz at 128x256 pixels, a single 4 s sweep per measurement, so a limited signal-to-noise ratio; as lip tension rose the response to the same driving fell. The artificial-lip Q of 8 to 10 is quoted from Cullen et al. 2000 and the glycerine-filled lip's 4 to 6 against 'typically 1.4-1.6' for real lips from Gazengel et al. ISMA 2007: second-hand. The lip is formed into an embouchure and loaded by the mouthpiece and the driving cavity, so every number is APPARATUS-EFFECTIVE. The Goldade 1997 flange slope (about 2.5 kPa) and the 45 kPa Takemoto value belong to the same class and are not in these rows.

column4: Bridge admittance of 10 preference-rated violins (hammer at the G-string corner, laser vibrometer at the E-string corner, strings damped, no chin or shoulder rest, neck on a foam block) and the frequencies of the five signature modes across the ten: A0 271 +- 6 Hz (range 262-281), A1 460 +- 17 (439-496), CBR 396 +- 16 (368-412), B1- 477 +- 15 (452-502), B1+ 522 +- 16 (501-557); A1/A0 1.64 +- 0.06; B1+ minus A1 62 +- 17 Hz (33-94); B1- minus CBR 80 +- 17 Hz (51-109) (a population range of a violin body's five lowest modes; no Q and no amplitudes in the text)
column14: C. Saitis, C. Fritz, B. L. Giordano and G. P. Scavone, Bridge admittance measurements of 10 preference-rated violins, Proc. Acoustics 2012, Nantes, pp.3599-3604 (the PDF is paginated 3605-3610); read in the HAL PDF, no licence printed. Ten violins: Storioni 1799, Sderci 1964, Gagliano 1770-75, a German 1787, Kaul 1933, a Canadian 2005, a Chinese 2006, Guarini 1877, a French 2009 and an unknown German; the standard deviations and ranges are across these ten, not measurement errors. The per-violin mode frequencies are plotted (Fig. 1b) and not tabulated; the overlaid admittances (Fig. 2, axis 200-5000 Hz, 'Admittance (dB)' with no reference unit stated) are figures and were not read. A bridge-corner to bridge-corner transfer admittance in the Jansson manner, not a driving-point at the bass foot. There is no Guarneri del Gesu among the ten (the one named in the introduction belongs to Bissinger's separate set). The paper finds no preference-related trend; it is not a quality ranking.

column4: Impact-hammer modal analysis (595 points, accelerometer on the bridge top, instruments on foam pillows) of named old and new violins from Martin Schleske's shop: B1 frequency of 11 old violins in Hz (Rogeri 16xx 500, Vuillaume 1872 506, Stradivari 1712 513/524, Bergonzi 519, Montagnana 1729 519, Stradivari 1721 517/527, Rivolta 1837 524, Stradivari 1727 533, Grancino 1699 541, J. Guarneri del Gesu 1733 544, J. Guarneri filius Andreae 1706 565); mean modal damping averaged over all modes of 16 instruments 1.1 to 1.5 percent (J. Guarneri del Gesu 1733 1.2 percent, Stradivari 1712 1.5, 1721 1.1, 1727 1.5, six of his own violins 1.2 to 1.4), falling about a factor 0.7 per decade of frequency; the four lowest modes of the Schreiber Stradivari 1712 A0 286, C2 409, T1 448, B1 524 Hz
column14: M. Schleske, Empirical tools in contemporary violin making: Part I. Analysis of design, materials, varnish and normal modes, Catgut Acoustical Society Journal Series II vol. 4 no. 5, May 2002, pp.43-64; read in the author-hosted PDF (CAS copyright, no licence printed). Tables 2 and 3 and Fig. 13; Appendix C for the conditions (foam rubber pillows at the end blocks, hammer PCB 86C80, accelerometer 0.5 g on the G-string side of the bridge top, STAR modal analysis, 4096 samples, 3.2 kHz). Damping is 'half the 3 dB bandwidth normalized to the mode frequency', i.e. a damping ratio zeta, so Q = 1/(2 zeta) is 33 to 45 (my conversion); it is the MEAN OVER ALL MODES, not the signature modes alone, and the signature modes radiate more (Bissinger) so their own damping is probably higher. Schleske's names T1 and B1 correspond to Bissinger's B1- and B1+ (inferred from Saitis 2012's footnote 1 and Krishnadas 2026), C2 to CBR. A1 'varies very little around a value just below 500 Hz'. The Stradivari 1712 and 1721 B1 values are split in two by fingerboard coupling. No uncertainty is printed; whether the violins were strung and how the strings were damped is not stated in what was read.

column4: Resonance profile of a Joseph Guarneri del Gesu of 1733 against a Stradivari of 1712: the del Gesu's T1 at 433 Hz and B1 at 544 Hz are far further apart than the Stradivari's (T1 448, B1 524 from Part I), and its T1 below 500 Hz is the strongest-radiating mode in the lower range (a measured Guarneri del Gesu violin: mode frequencies and mean damping 1.2 percent, no admittance table)
column14: M. Schleske, Empirical tools in contemporary violin making: Part II. Psychoacoustic analysis and use of acoustical tools, CAS Journal Series II vol. 4 no. 6, November 2002, p.46 Fig. 2 caption (author-hosted PDF, CAS copyright). Also, from a search-engine excerpt of Schleske's web page (the page itself returned HTTP 503 twice and was not read): 'the frequency interval between the two main corpus resonances (T1 and B1) is significantly larger in instruments by Guarneri del Gesu' after modal analyses of various violins by Stradivari. Which Guarneri del Gesu violin it is is not stated in what was read; Part I Table 2 lists 'J. Guarneri del Gesu 1733'. The 433 Hz and 544 Hz are printed in a figure caption, not tabulated, and carry no uncertainty. Not il Cannone (1743).

column4: Experimental modal analysis (230-point impact grid on the front plate, one fixed accelerometer, strung violins with undamped strings at tension, no chin or shoulder rest) of two violins before and after varnishing: unvarnished violin 1 A0 281 Hz (damping 10.0 percent of critical), B1- 476 Hz (9.6), B1+ 548 Hz (8.1); violin 2 A0 280 (9.0), B1- 451 (7.1), B1+ 540 (5.0); spirit-varnished violin 1 A0 277 (5.2), B1- 492 (4.6), B1+ 598 (4.1); oil-varnished violin 2 A0 276 (6.4), B1- 419 (17.0, above the authors' 10 percent linearity limit), B1+ 534 (5.1)
column14: E. B. Skrodzka, B. B. J. Linde and A. Krupa, Modal parameters of two violins with different varnish layers and subjective evaluation of their sound quality, Archives of Acoustics 38(1) 2013 pp.75-81, Table 3; read in the open PDF (journals.pan.pl). Two instruments the authors call 'not excellent'. The damping column is printed as the percentage of the critical damping, which is 3 to 15 times the 1.1-1.5 percent all-mode mean of Schleske and gives Q = 1/(2 zeta) of 3 to 12 (my conversion): the two sets disagree by an order of magnitude and the difference is probably the setup (undamped strings on, a modal fit to a front-plate response), so treat it as a number for THIS setup, not a population value. No measurement uncertainty is printed.

column4: Repeatability and humidity sensitivity of violin bridge admittance on one violin (Yamaha V-5 4/4, 2009; hammer on the G-string side of the bridge; velocity by laser below the bridge foot on the top plate, or on the opposite side of the bridge; rubber-band suspension; strings damped with nylon ribbon; ten removals and reinstallations): normalized total variation (sum of standard deviation over mean) 0.1035 (240-880 Hz), 0.2068 (460-490 Hz), 0.1136 (540-580 Hz) for the below-foot method and 0.0468, 0.0397, 0.0515 for the opposite-side method; humidity 85 to 25 percent RH shifts A0 by about 2 percent, CBR and B1- by more than 8 percent, B1+ by 5.3 percent; this violin's B1+ is near 560 Hz, A1 near 480, A2 at 825 Hz
column14: A. Piacsek and S. Lowery, Experimental uncertainty in measurements of violin impulse response, Proc. 10th Convention of the European Acoustics Association (Forum Acusticum 2023), Turin, starting p.3423, Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 Unported; read in the open PDF. The only open violin driving-point-style admittance I found (velocity of the top plate just below the bass-side bridge foot, hammer at the same side); the figure axis is printed 'decibels re 1 N/m/s', which is not an admittance unit and is kept as printed. One cheap violin, so its mode frequencies are not a population value; its use is the size of the measurement and environment error bars (about 5 percent between repeated installations by the better method, about 10 to 20 percent by the other, and a humidity shift of several percent in the plate-dominated modes).

column4: Signature modes of a violin body without neck or soundpost, measured (George Stoppani): A0 243 Hz, CBR 394, B1- 403, B1+ 562, against Colin Gough's simplified finite-element values 262, 376, 397, 558 Hz; and the mode frequencies of an early modal-testing example: CBR 436, B1- 454, B1+ 538 Hz (body-only reference for a model that has no neck or soundpost)
column14: J. Woodhouse, The acoustics of the violin: a review, Reports on Progress in Physics 77 (2014) 115901, Figs. 16 and 18 captions; read in the Cambridge accepted manuscript (https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk/handle/1810/245817, 96 pages). The caption says the left pair of each mode is measured and the right pair computed; the assignment of 243 to the measurement and 262 to the FE value follows the layout of the extracted caption and was not checked on the figure image. column4: Open measured force-compression law of PIANO HAMMER FELT with a stated protocol (not a mallet head for bars): the four-parameter hereditary law (instantaneous stiffness F0, exponent p, hereditary amplitude eps, relaxation time tau0) fitted to dynamic loading and unloading loops from a purpose-built rig. Renner A1 on a 4.3 mm string piece at 0.35, 0.54 and 0.78 m/s: F0 400 N/mm^p, p 2.4, eps 0.51, tau0 400 us from ONE parameter set for all three loops. Abel A1 at 0.7 m/s: eps 0.69, tau0 250 us, with F0 and p depending on what the felt strikes (flat sensor 480 and 2.7; strings of 4.3, 2.25 and 1.25 mm: 400 and 2.3, 330 and 2.0, 270 and 1.8); the rig's added mass 37.5 g and gap-sensor aperture 2.0 mm
column14: A. Stulov and A. Magi, Piano hammer testing device, Proc. Estonian Acad. Sci. Eng. 6(4) 2000 pp.259-267, read in the open PDF at kirj.ee (eng-4-2000-259-267), which served it to a script with the honest User-Agent on 2026-10-21; no licence is stated on the PDF, so numbers only; no page, table layout or figure is reproduced. Values read from the text layer AND the rendered pp.264-265 images (the Fig. 6 legend gives the three speeds; the parameter sets are the text under Figs. 6 and 7). Protocol: the hammer strikes a string piece fixed on a piezoelectric force sensor (calibrated by dropping roller bearings, 18.3 N/V); felt compression from an infrared gap sensor behind a flag on a titanium-tube shank (calibrated by a free fall at 1.52 m/s); the law is fitted by simulating the strike with the hammer mass plus the rig's 37.5 g. CAVEATS: a device paper demonstrating the rig on TWO hammers; hammer masses are not printed; no fit goodness or uncertainty ('confirms the theory fairly well'); F0 and p move with the string diameter, so a pair without its contact geometry is not a datum (u in mm, F in N: F0 is N per mm^p). PIANO HAMMERS ARE WOOL FELT on a wood core, not the yarn, cord, rubber, phenolic or acrylic heads of mallet-percussion bars: this is the right LAW and a plausible order of magnitude for soft felt-like heads, not a measurement of any of them. It answers the felt-coupon-hunt gap (kirj.ee gave the PDF where HAL did not).

Against the measured Renner and Abel A1 hammers of Stulov and Magi 2000 (n = 1) they give p 3.7 against 2.3 to 2.7, eps 0.99 against 0.51 and 0.69, tau 2.7 us against 250 to 400 us; only Q0 (191 against 196 N/mm^p from 400 x 0.49) and the mass agree. As printed eps(n) = 0.9894 + 8.8e-5 n^2 exceeds 1 for n >= 11, which makes Q0 = F0 (1 - eps) negative: a misprint or a different definition, NOT resolved, so none of the five fits is to be used without reading the source. The contact-time formula is a method: with p = 1.5 it gives 3.218 (m^2/(K^2 V))^(1/5) (arithmetic of mine), the 3.21 of Doutaut and Chaigne 1994 Eq. 3, and 0.16 ms for their boxwood head at 2.1 m/s.

column4: Width of the flute embouchure hole left uncovered by the lower lip: about 6 mm at C4 falling to 3.5 mm at G6, typically 1 to 2 mm less than the jet length (Coltman 1966, quoted by Fletcher 1975 p.234, left column); the flute cards take it linear in semitones between those two endpoints as the open strip of the window's lip cover (D4 5.8387, G4 5.4355, A5 4.3065 mm)
column14: N. H. Fletcher, Acoustical correlates of flute performance technique, JASA 57(1) 1975 pp.233-237 (ANU open repository copy), p.234, quoting J. W. Coltman, Resonance and sounding frequencies of the flute, JASA 40 (1966) 99-107, which plotted it for his players; the original is not read here, so this is a secondhand value. Linear in semitones between the two quoted endpoints is mine, not the source's. Bracket, not an input: Dickens 2007 (PhD thesis, UNSW, section 7.1, printed p.104, Fig. 7.1) reports about 25 percent of the hole covered for one flutist miming C4 to F7, which on the 9.874 mm hole leaves 7.41 mm open. Same-quantity check, never an input: Vauthrin 2015 (thesis, eq. 2.13 and Fig. 2.17) measures the head's end correction 28.8 mm without a flutist and about 43 to 60 mm with one. The strip lies against the hole's far edge, the lip covering the rest from the player's side, with the player's face 1.8 mm behind the lip's edge (fletcher-1975-flute-lip-emergence-setback); the lip's thickness and the lip plate's shape are not represented (unknowns.tsv of flute-boehm-silver-bfoot-boehm1871).

column4: How far behind the lower lip's edge over the flute's embouchure hole the jet leaves the player's lips: Fletcher 1975 (p.234, left column) compares Coltman's uncovered widths with his own players' jet lengths (measured on profile photographs from the jet's apparent point of emergence at the lips to the target edge, p.234) and finds the uncovered width typically 1 to 2 mm less than the jet length; his p.235 fit of the jet length carries a dead interval of 1.8 mm effectively shielded from the acoustic field. The flute cards stand the player's face, a rigid half-plane through the bore's axis, 1.8 mm behind the lip's edge on the head's outer surface; the range ends, 1 and 2 mm, are rendered as brackets
column14: N. H. Fletcher, Acoustical correlates of flute performance technique, JASA 57(1) 1975 pp.233-237 (ANU open repository copy): p.234 defines the jet length and quotes Coltman 1966's uncovered widths as typically 1-2 mm less than it; p.235 Eq. 5 and the text after it give the 1.8 mm dead interval. The setback is the difference of two photographed lengths for different players (Coltman's and Fletcher's), so it is a range; the cards take the one value the source fits to it, 1.8 mm. The face as a plane through the jet's emergence point, normal to the jet and through the bore's axis, is the model's, not the source's. Same-quantity check, never an input: Vauthrin 2015 (thesis, eq. 2.13, Fig. 2.17, eq. 2.14) measures the head's end correction 28.8 mm without a flutist and about 43 to 60 mm with one.

column4: Radiation inertance of a flute-like opening with an inclined plane standing for the player's face (Ernoult, de la Cuadra and Fabre 2018): m_r = rho cot(beta/4)/(4 pi r_o) + m_r0, with r_o = sqrt(S_o/pi) the opening's equivalent radius, m_r0 the inertance with no plane, beta = pi a flange and 2 pi no plane (eq. 24, p.13; eqs. 32-33, pp.14-15); measured against finite elements on a quena notch, the law's C = rho/(4 pi r_o) gives about 10 where about 7 is measured (p.13); valid for k r_o below about 0.25 (p.15); a real flutist's beta is not measured (section 5.1, p.15). A same-quantity check on the face's computed static mass, never an input
column14: A. Ernoult, P. de la Cuadra, B. Fabre, An inclined plane: a simple model for the acoustic influence of the musician's face on the radiation of flute-like instruments, Acta Acustica united with Acustica 104(3) 2018 pp.496-508 (HAL preprint hal-01943166; page numbers are the preprint's). Used only to compare the face's computed static mass with the law at the face angle the model's geometry has locally (a plane normal to the outer surface, beta about pi/2), which is the model's reading and not a measured player angle: at the lip's edge the solved face adds 0.81, 0.88 and 0.93 of the law's inertance at D4, G4 and A5, between the law and the law scaled to the measured notch.

column4: Drumstick crush across the grain: shagbark hickory at 12% moisture content from Wood Handbook Table 5-3a, side hardness 8,400 N (the load to embed an 11.28-mm ball to one-half its diameter, average of radial and tangential penetrations; footnote d: the true hickories' side hardness is from Bendtsen and Ethington (1975)) and compression perpendicular to grain 12,100 kPa (fiber stress at proportional limit), with the mockernut, pignut and shellbark side hardness (8,800, 9,500 and 8,100 N) kept as the stated spread, admitted from 15 to 25 C
column14: Read by SandyBass for .372 (ruling 7476 item 6) in the full FPL-GTR-282 (2021) PDF, treesearch 62200 (sha256 f0b488c5637614d8e69a07abf796f9e32d7a8df956ee75ab5cc5f64f3bd5ee6f, 99 MB; the chapter-5 URL returned an HTML block page): Table 5-3a on page 5-5 with footnotes a and d on page 5-8, the Strength Properties definitions of hardness and compressive stress perpendicular to grain from page 5-3, Table 5-6 (average coefficients of variation 20% for side hardness and 28% for compression perpendicular to grain) and Table 5-15 (compressive strength perpendicular to grain at proportional limit -35% at +50 C relative to 20 C at 10% moisture content; no temperature effect on hardness is tabulated). The pack stores the tabulated load. The kit's shaft-on-edge crush (fs-vkplate shaft.rs) reads it as a mean pressure over the projected area of the half-embedded ball, pi (5.64 mm)^2, 84.1 MPa, and crushes at that mean pressure on the Hertz contact area (Thornton 1997), half the edge's truncation of the shaft, so at a given crush depth it is the lower of the two readings of the same datum. The compression perpendicular to grain is stated with every shaft strike and not used: it is where a plate-loaded block begins to crush, a seventh of the hardness pressure.

column4: Hot-wire velocity profiles u/u_max against y/h 1.5 mm from the flue exit of an alto recorder (windway 70.5 mm long, uniformly converging from 2 mm to 1 mm, chamfered exit) at captioned Re 212 and 666: left- and right-flank positions at u/u_max 0.10 to 0.95, read from Segoufin 2000 Fig. 5.13 after van den Tillart 1999
column14: C. Segoufin, PhD thesis, Univ. Paris 6, 2000 (open PDF on lam.jussieu.fr), Fig. 5.13 p. 87 and text p. 86, after J. van den Tillart, TU/e report R1491S (1999, not located online); facts only. Digitised from a scanned figure: the PDF embeds each panel as a 141 ppi greyscale bitmap. Raster trace calibrated on each panel's own frame and ticks (scan skew about 0.3 deg fitted per frame line; tick residuals at most 0.013 h and 0.003 u/u_max top, 0.008 h and 0.004 bottom); the dotted best-fit parabola is excluded and the traced stroke was checked against the bitmap; traced peaks 0.9999 and 1.0000. Reading error (OD17): tick residual plus half a pixel, u/u_max 0.005 and y/h 0.019 (top), 0.007 and 0.012 (bottom). Not read below u/u_max 0.10, where the stroke meets the baseline and ticks. REYNOLDS NUMBER NOT SETTLED BY THE TEXT: the Fig. 5.13 caption and p. 86 give Re = h U_e/nu, U_e the inlet speed 'deduced from the hot-wire centre speed' (Goorman 2000, not available), and the chapter's h is the exit height (p. 86 h_e 2 mm, h_s 1 mm; Fig. 5.14 2h in, h out; Fig. 5.10 Re_h = h U_e/nu = 666 is U0 = 10 m/s into a 1 mm channel). But Fig. 5.14, the RNS-p counterpart the text compares at the same Re 666, defines Re = h U_e/(2 nu), the half height of the RNS-p appendix. Reading I (as captioned): exit bulk Re_h = 2 Re = 424 and 1332. Reading II (Fig. 5.14 convention): 4 Re = 848 and 2664. Both are carried and every grade reports both. Other defects: the profiles are 1.5 mm (1.5 h) downstream of the exit, not at it; chamfered exit; hot-wire size and calibration not stated; no blowing pressure, so no U(P). VALIDATION target, held out, for the developing-flow windway law of pexfp.135.4; never a model input.

column4: The gas in a played flute's bore: carbon dioxide about 2.5 percent, which alone flattens the notes by about 12 cents; temperature about 26.5 C at the upper end to 25.8 C at the lower end of the flute in a 21 C room, which with its water vapour sharpens them by 17 to 19.5 cents. The three flute cards take the mean 26.15 C (299.30 K), 101325 Pa, saturated, CO2 2.5 percent dry and O2 18.5 percent dry: wet mole fractions N2 0.7546, O2 0.1788, Ar 0.0090, CO2 0.0242, H2O 0.0334
column14: J. W. Coltman, The acoustics of the flute, Physics Today 21(11), November 1968, pp.25-32, p.27 (AIP open online copy), in the passage on alteration of the natural resonance, where he reports measurements on a flute. Not in the source and mine: the mean of the two end temperatures; saturation of the bore air (the passage only says water vapour is included; the shared breath pack coltman-nederveen-fletcher-woodwind-breath takes saturation, and my own ideal-gas sum for 26.5 and 25.8 C saturated against 21 C air gives +22 and +20 cents against his 17 to 19.5, the room's humidity being unstated); the water-vapour fraction, Magnus p_sat 3385 Pa at 26.15 C; and O2 18.5 percent dry with the N2 to Ar ratio, paired from that pack's own bracket because Coltman gives no O2.
